Validating the methods of Leibold et al. (2010) and Peres-Neto et al. (2012)

Source: vignettes/articles/validation-gradient.Rmd
validation-gradient.Rmd

The functions phylo_vector(), trait_partition() and node_test() are translations of MATLAB code from the supplements of these articles. We checked them in three ways. Each help page lists the differences between the text of the article and the code.

Comparison with the original code

We ran the MATLAB code in Octave on the numerical example of Appendix A of Peres-Neto et al. (2012) and on simulated data. The supplement lacks the functions eigen and WeightedMeanVar, which we wrote. Weighted coordinates, correlations, Moran’s eigenvector maps and the raw and adjusted fractions agreed to within 1e-13. Correlations also agreed with ade4::fourthcorner(). The package does not include the maps, as those of adespatial::dbmem() are the same as the ones of the supplement.

Type I error and power

The script data-raw/validation_gradient.R follows the simulations of the article, with 1000 data sets and 999 permutations (100 sites and 50 species, one environmental variable). The article stacks the two null distributions and uses alpha / 2, shown here as “stacked”. Rates near 0.05 are expected for a true null hypothesis, with a standard error near 0.007.

Trait and environment (Table 4 of the article), with the correlation inside phylo_vector(). The package has no function for this test, which is available in ade4::fourthcorner():

Case Tolerance Stacked, article Stacked, here Larger p, here
Random environment (Table 1) 1 0.028 0.039 0.051

With tolerances of 20 and 60, which the article does not report for Tables 1 and 2, the larger p-value gave rates from 0.037 to 0.055. The test of the final vector after a significant global test kept these rates, because the global test comes first. A test of that vector alone is not valid, as it was chosen to fit the predictor.

Weights of the eigenvectors

The correlation between the vector and the trait that generated the data depends on how the eigenvectors are weighted. The text uses correlations and the code their absolute values.

Tolerance PEV with absolute values, here PEV in Table 3 PEV with signs, here PEV-B, here PEV-B in Table 3
1 0.480 0.514 0.685 0.698 0.676
20 0.455 0.526 0.722 0.707 0.703
60 0.473 0.508 0.740 0.715 0.688

Absolute values give about what the article reports for PEV, which suggests that its Table 3 used them (this is our interpretation). With signs, PEV matches PEV-B, so the gain of the Brownian vectors reported in the article may come from this difference.

Partition

Table 5 uses the logistic generator of Appendix C. The appendix leaves out the intercepts and the scale of the slopes, so we took them from the simulation code of Ives & Helmus (2011): intercepts from N(0, 0.5), slopes with a standard deviation of 1 among species, and presences from a uniform draw. Neither the article nor the appendix says how the two vectors were obtained. The fractions of Table 5 agree with the vectors that generated the data, and its rejection rates for E and S agree with the global test of phylo_vector(), so the table below combines both (data-raw/validation_table5.R, 1000 data sets, 999 permutations). The values of the article are in parentheses:

Scenario [E, S] [a] [b] [c] Rejection of E Rejection of S
I 0.490 (0.478) 0.223 (0.216) 0.043 (0.069) 0.223 (0.193) 0.706 (0.687) 0.710 (0.679)
II 0.473 (0.589) 0.008 (0.061) 0.458 (0.488) 0.007 (0.036) 0.700 (0.750) 0.705 (0.751)
III 0.383 (0.349) 0.239 (0.234) 0.030 (0.036) 0.114 (0.079) 0.691 (0.701) 0.592 (0.418)
IV 0.047 (0.032) 0.023 (0.015) 0.000 (0.001) 0.024 (0.016) 0.043 (0.051) 0.047 (0.061)
V 0.524 (0.457) 0.219 (0.202) 0.049 (0.054) 0.255 (0.201) 0.683 (0.597) 0.724 (0.637)
VI 0.518 (0.440) 0.217 (0.201) 0.051 (0.063) 0.251 (0.176) 0.707 (0.632) 0.697 (0.627)
VII 0.549 (0.396) 0.255 (0.194) 0.041 (0.000) 0.253 (0.202) 0.700 (0.562) 0.708 (0.597)

The pattern among scenarios is the same, and scenarios I, III and IV are the closest. Three choices are ours. In scenario III, the N(0, 1) error of Appendix C has no effect on a gradient from -15 to 15, so we added it to y with unit variance, and only in the analysis. In scenarios V and VI, x is in random order along the transect, as otherwise it is correlated with space. In scenario II we kept the text, and the gradients seem more correlated than those of the article, as fractions a and c are smaller.

Three parts remain different. The share of the compositional component is near 0.62 in all scenarios, whereas the article gives 0.39 to 0.94, so that value must depend on something that the appendix does not describe. Scenario VII has a larger b than the zero of the article, probably because the maps here are orthogonal only without site weights. The rejection of [E, S] is 0.71 to 0.91, against 0.77 to 0.84, here as the rejection of either gradient, which gives 0.085 in scenario IV against 0.055 in the article. Rejections of a and c, with vectors estimated only after a significant global test, were 0.66 to 0.71 and 0.48 to 0.72 outside scenarios II and IV, against 0.56 to 0.70 and 0.30 to 0.60 in the article; in scenario II they were zero, against 0.29 and 0.25.

Following the demonstration script of the authors instead, with a vector fixed in advance and predictors without relation to the data, rejection rates of the larger p-value were 0.023 to 0.028, because both null hypotheses are true. With environment and space acting, the global test for environment passed in 37% of the data sets. In those, the rejection rate was 0.99 for fraction a and 0.03 for fraction c, as expected for a vector estimated for environment alone.

Tests of the fractions

The code of the authors permutes environment and space with the same order of sites and compares fractions a and c themselves with their null values, so each is compared with what is expected when neither set matters. The fraction is not a pivotal statistic: when the other set explains much, the observed fraction is a share of what that set leaves, and the null fraction is a share of everything, so the test loses its power. Up to version 0.6.0 the package did the same; trait_partition() now tests a and c with the share of the component that the other set leaves unexplained, which is a monotone function of the partial F statistic, under the same permutations (Anderson & Legendre 1999 found that permutation of raw data with a pivotal statistic has the right size except with outliers in the covariable). The shared fraction b is tested with shared_null, following adespatial::envspace.test() (Bauman et al. 2019): env is replaced by surrogates that keep its spatial autocorrelation, built by Moran spectral randomisation (Wagner & Dray 2015) or by moves of the whole map on a grid, while the response and space stay fixed.

The script data-raw/validation_fractions.R measures type I error and power on a complete grid of 8 by 8 sites, with space holding the six broadest Moran’s eigenvector maps, 20 species with Gaussian responses to a gradient that combines the environment (weight alpha) and a smooth field in the span of space (weight beta), 199 permutations and 500 data sets per scenario, with seeds separate from the 200 data sets used to choose the statistic and the null models. The environment is independent noise (iid), a smooth field in the span of space plus noise (broad), or a field at scales that space does not hold (fine). In the last scenario the composition follows another trait than the one analysed, so the null hypothesis of the permutation of species is true for every fraction. Rates at the 5% level have standard errors of 0.010 or less; a true null hypothesis is marked by an asterisk.

The old test never rejected a when space acted and the environment did not, nor c in the mirror case, and had little power for a weak effect of the environment beside space. The new statistic holds the level there and in the tuning run gave the same rates as permutation of the residuals of the reduced model (Freedman & Lane 1983) and as permutation of the predictor of interest alone, which do not support site_permutations and the permutation of species. Three limits remain. When the environment has spatial structure at scales that space does not hold, the free permutation of sites rejects a too often (0.114), because the residuals keep spatial structure that the environment matches by chance; moves of the whole map hold the level (0.014). When a strong, spatially structured environment acts alone, the free permutation rejects c in 10% of the data sets: the species respond to the environment with Gaussian curves, the linear fit leaves a spatially structured remainder, and space explains it, which the larger p-value does not take as significant (0.024). The column grid moves both sets together, which was what site_permutations did up to version 0.6.1: that test of c was liberal when the environment explained much (0.190) and never rejected when the environment was spatially structured, because it compares space with an environment that no longer explains the response. The next section measures what the moves should move. With a trait unrelated to the composition, the permutation of sites rejects a in about half the data sets and the larger p-value holds the level, as intended. The permutation of species alone, with 20 species, is slightly liberal when nothing acts (0.066 to 0.080 with either statistic), and the larger p-value is not.

A second generator (data-raw/validation_fractions_check.R: counts, a grid of 10 by 10 sites, 8 Moran’s eigenvector maps, 200 data sets) gave larger values for these two limits. With a hidden field that space holds only in part, free permutations rejected a in 21% of the data sets (larger p-value: 2%), and with a structured environment acting alone they rejected c in 25% (larger p-value: 7.5%). So p_max, not the p-value of sites alone, is the one to read.

What the moves of a grid should move

A restricted permutation keeps the spatial structure of what it moves, so the question is which set to move in each test. The script data-raw/validation_fractions_null.R compares, with torus_permutations(), moves of both sets together (the behaviour up to version 0.6.1), of env alone and of space alone, against free permutations, on the first generator above (300 data sets, seeds separate from the holdout), and then checks the choice on the second generator (200 data sets) through trait_partition() itself, which from this version moves env alone for ab, a and the semipartials of env, space alone for bc, c and the semipartials of space, and both for abc. Rates at the 5% level with the p-value of sites, and in parentheses the larger p-value where the p-value of sites alone rejects 8% or more of the data sets under a true null hypothesis; standard errors are 0.013 or less for rates near the level on the first generator and 0.018 or less on the second.

For a, moving env alone holds the level in every null scenario of both generators, where free permutations reach 0.097 and 0.200 with an environment structured at scales outside space, and moving both together is conservative there (0.010); its power is the same. For c, moving space alone holds the level where free permutations reach 0.080 and 0.236 with a strong, structured environment acting alone, and where moving both together reaches 0.220 with a strong environment without structure. The premise that moves of the grid barely change what Moran’s eigenvector maps explain did not hold: on the grid of 8 by 8, a moved map has on average 30% of its variance outside the span of the six maps in place. The power of the restricted test of c depends on the question. It is complete when the species follow a field in the span of space, and 0.25 to 0.28 when they follow a field of exponential covariance that space holds only in part (free permutations: 0.975 to 0.980), because the maps moved around the grid explain such a field about as well as the maps in place. That test asks whether the maps in space explain more than the same maps elsewhere on the grid, not whether the remainder of the environment has any spatial structure; for the second question, use free permutations and read p_max.

The shared fraction b, with env replaced by free permutations of its values, by Moran spectral randomisations (MSR, shared_null = "msr") and by moves of the whole map (shared_null = "sites" with torus_permutations()), by permutations of species, and with the larger p-value. Tested is the number of data sets, out of 500, where env was related to space and b was tested with the MSR:

b is left untested when env is unrelated to space at the 5% level, which happened in 94% to 97% of the data sets with an iid environment and in all those with structure outside space; the rates above leave those data sets out, and with fewer than 30 of them they say little. With an environment that is spatially structured but has no effect, free permutations of env reject b in 48% of the data sets, the Moran spectral randomisation holds the level (0.056), and moves on the grid are liberal (0.110), which we did not expect and leave as a limit of that null model. The permutation of species asks whether the trait matters, not whether the shared structure is spurious, so it rejects when space acts through the trait; conversely, with a trait unrelated to the composition, the randomisation of env alone rejects often and only the larger p-value holds the level. Power is complete when the environment alone acts and moderate when space also acts on its own.

The daphniids of Leibold et al. (2010)

The data set daphniids rebuilds the data of the article from the public survey. With the larger p-value, no predictor is significant at any node, as species permutations have little power with 13 species. The article permutes rows and columns together, which node_test() gives as p_joint. Rates of rejection per node at the 5% level (one Yule tree of 24 species, 60 sites, 300 data sets, 99 permutations, data-raw/validation_node.R):

What acts Sites Species Larger p Joint
Neither 0.053 0.049 0.021 0.050
Environment 0.777 0.049 0.049 0.764
Phylogeny 0.046 0.050 0.021 0.050
Both 0.803 0.073 0.073 0.795

The joint test is valid only when neither acts. With the environment alone it behaves as the permutation of sites, so it does not separate an effect of the environment from an association between environment and phylogeny.

In the daphniids, the joint test with 999 permutations found fewer predictors than sites alone at the 0.05 level (PHEQ, AV_DEP, DOC, TN_TP and PTL at four nodes, with none left after the false discovery rate). It therefore did not recover Figure 3a better. With sites alone, at a level of 0.05 without correction and 999 permutations, environmental results compare with Figure 3a as follows:

Node Figure 3a Here
retrocurva, parvula, catawba COND, NTL COND, NTL
Same plus pulicaria, pulex AV_DEP, PHEQ AV_DEP, PHEQ
longispina, galeata, rosea AV_DEP, ELEV AV_DEP, ELEV
All species TN:TP, AV_DEP, ELEV, DOC, COLOR COLOR, DOC, AV_DEP
All Daphnia except laevis, dubia AV_DEP, PHEQ, ELEV, DOC AV_DEP, PHEQ, ELEV, DOC, NTL, TN_TP
Clade with ambigua ELEV ELEV, TN_TP
retrocurva, parvula PHEQ, AV_DEP AV_DEP
pulicaria, pulex ELEV, NTL none
galeata, rosea COLOR, DOC none
laevis, dubia COND NTL, PHEQ, PTL, TN_TP

Nodes with rare species differ most: D. laevis and D. rosea occur in one and two lakes of the rebuilt set. Biogeographic results differ more (no match at most nodes), which we expected, because the article does not give the area of each lake and we approximated rivers by longitude.
